title: Boys at Risk: Online Gaming, Sports Betting, and Addiction
author: Emily Harrison
summary: Emily Harrison, a mother of two boys and a digital media advocate, argues that one of the biggest drivers of the struggles of young men is addictive screen media aimed at boys, especially online gaming and gambling. Citing ScreenStrong founder Melanie Hempe's term the Basement Generation and addiction psychiatrist Michelle Dirst, she describes how loot boxes, in-game currencies and sports-betting promotions such as risk-free bets prime young brains for compulsive behavior. Gaming addiction is recognized by the WHO but remains only a condition for further study in the DSM-5, so treatment and insurance coverage lag. IFS data show nearly one in four young men gambling daily, mostly alongside daily gaming. Harrison urges parents not to wait the roughly 17 years it takes research to become practice, and to talk about gambling the way they talk about drugs.
points: Online gaming platforms embed gambling-adjacent mechanics, such as loot boxes and virtual currencies, that train boys toward addictive habits before they ever reach sports-betting apps.
Experts warn that youth gaming and gambling, especially when combined with AI, could eventually look like the scale of the opioid crisis, with gambling most associated with suicide among addictions.
Because gaming addiction lacks a formal DSM-5 diagnosis, families face thin treatment options and little insurance coverage.
IFS survey data link daily gambling and daily gaming among young men with demoralization and loneliness.
Parents should learn what gambling features their sons' games contain, discuss gambling like drug use, and not wait for slow research to confirm the risk.
quotes: But one of the biggest culprits is the proliferation of addictive screen media marketed toward boys, specifically online gaming and gambling.

As young girls have spent ever increasing time scrolling social media feeds, boys have retreated to playing online video games in basements, virtually connected to friends, as well as strangers who care little about their well-being.
Baked into the operating systems of online gaming platforms today are gambling and gambling-adjacent features that prime the underdeveloped brain for addictive habits.

Loot boxes are also a popular digital tool among video game developers, used in a similar fashion to a slot machine. Most players will gain nothing of substantial value for game play, while the allure of winning big dangles in front of hopeful players chasing the ever elusive “rare” item.
Most Gen X and elder Millennial parents are unaware of the inherent gambling features in modern games, as these were absent from games that they may have grown up playing in the 1990s.
After all, parents cannot wait nearly two decades to find out if these platforms are safe for their boys. An entire childhood—and future—hangs in the balance.

In the last five years, Les Bernal, National Director for Stop Predatory Gambling, told me he’s seen an uptick in teenage boys attending Gamblers Anonymous meetings. “Parents need to talk to their kids about gambling in the same way they talk about drug use,” he cautioned.
